title: Parikshit's seven days
hookLine: a king told he has seven days to live spends them listening: the fear of death runs even in the wise
carry: abhinivesha: even the wise cling to life
tomorrow: an arrow shot in the dark. when does it land?
last: RAGA, DVESHA — THE PULL AND THE PUSH.

lines: A DEAD SNAKE ON A SAGE.
THE KING SITS BY THE GANGA.
cards: King Parikshit, Arjuna's grandson, is out hunting, tired and thirsty. He finds a sage sitting in deep meditation who doesn't answer him.

In a flash of anger, the king hangs a dead snake around the sage's shoulders and leaves. The sage's young son hears of it and curses him: in seven days, the serpent Takshaka will bite him, and he will die.
Parikshit doesn't fight the curse. He gives his kingdom to his son and sits down on the bank of the Ganga.

teach.h: ONE QUESTION, SEVEN DAYS OF STORIES.
teach.b: Sages gather. Parikshit asks them one question: what should a person do who is about to die?
Then the young sage Shuka arrives, and for seven days he tells the king the Bhagavata Purana, story after story of God, while the king fasts and listens.

teach.h: LET GO OF 'I AM GOING TO DIE.'
teach.b: Near the end, Shuka tells him, in effect: let go of the thought, I am going to die. That's a creature's thinking. Unlike the body, you weren't born, and you won't be destroyed.
This is why many Hindus still hold a Bhagavat saptah, a seven-day reading of the whole text, and why families read scripture and say God's name beside someone near the end. Now Patanjali.
Sutra 2.9 names the fifth affliction: abhinivesha, clinging to life.

It is svarasa-vahi, flowing by its own momentum, like a river downhill, and established even in the wise. Vidushah api. The classical commentary hears in every creature the same wish: may I not stop being.
Even a just-hatched worm shrinks from danger. Notice who Parikshit is: a good king, saved by Krishna before he was born.
Wisdom alone doesn't empty the fear, and Patanjali doesn't shame anyone for it; he says the afflictions are undone by tracing them back to their source, and quieted by meditation.
Parikshit spent his last days on what doesn't die. Day to day, abhinivesha is rarely about dying. It's the grip on how things were: a house, a role, any small ending.

teach.h: THE SAME GRAB, IN SMALL ENDINGS.

how: Many Hindu communities hold a Bhagavat saptah, a seven-day recitation of the Bhagavata Purana that remembers the seven days Parikshit listened to Shuka. Near the end of life, families often read scripture and repeat God's name beside the dying person. Students of the Yoga Sutras study abhinivesha with the classical commentary.

o: flowing only when you push it hard
flowing by its own momentum, like a river
carried along by a teacher's guidance

games.q: the king, the sage and the sutra — tap the pairs.
p: seven days to live, spent listening
clinging to life, the wish to go on

s: the sutra says only the unlearned fear death
2.9 says the opposite: it is established even in the wise.
a Bhagavat saptah is a seven-day reading, after Parikshit's seven days
many Hindus still gather to hear the whole Bhagavata over a week.
the classical commentary reads a newborn's fear as memory of earlier deaths
a creature that has never died in this life already shrinks from death, so the commentary calls it a trace from before.

games.q: Parikshit learns he has seven days left. by sutra 2.9 and his story, what fits?
o: hunt down the sage's son and break the curse.
sit by the Ganga hearing about God: even the wise meet the fear with practice, not denial.
act as if nothing is happening; the wise feel no fear.
games.why: 2.9 says clinging to life is there even in the wise. Parikshit doesn't pretend; he spends the days on what doesn't die.

practice: Let the breath run on its own. On each out-breath, say a name silently: Ram, or Krishna, or Om, whichever name you love; if you don't pray, a word like peace.

Notice the little pause at the end of the out-breath, and whether something in you hurries to grab the next one. No need to hold it; let each breath come by itself. If anything feels uncomfortable, breathe normally.

wordCard.voice: Svarasa-vahi, flowing by its own momentum, like a river downhill. Abhinivesha, the clinging to going on, runs by itself this way, and stays even in the wise.

orig.note: Sanskrit abhiniveśa: settling into, clinging; in the Yoga Sutras, the clinging to life.

carryVoice: Your line: abhinivesha, even the wise cling to life. Parikshit spent his seven days on what doesn't die. Go gently; see you tomorrow.

Yoga Sutra 2.9 (abhinivesha: flowing by its own momentum, established even in the wise)
Yoga Bhashya on 2.9 (may I not cease to be; the newborn worm)
Yoga Sutra 2.10–2.11 (afflictions removed by tracing back and by meditation)
